lines: Part two: how do we choose labels that fit both the words and each other?
A hidden Markov model says: hidden tags generate the visible words.
Each tag depends only on the previous tag. That is the transition. Each word depends only on its own tag. That is the emission.
Careful with the direction: an emission is the probability of the word given the tag, not the tag given the word.
Take can fish, with two tags, noun and verb. Two words, two tags: four possible paths.
Each path is start, times emission, times transition, times emission.
Verb then noun: zero point four, times zero point seven, times zero point eight, times zero point six. That is zero point one three four four, the largest.
All four paths add up to zero point two four four eight, the probability of the words.
So zero point one three four four is a joint weight. The posterior is that divided by zero point two four four eight: about zero point five five.
Viterbi gets the same answer without listing every path.
At can: noun zero point two four, verb zero point two eight.
At fish, ending in noun: from noun, zero point oh seven two. From verb, zero point two two four. Keep verb, then multiply by the emission: zero point one three four four.
Ending in verb, the best predecessor is noun: zero point oh five oh four.
Pick the larger cell and follow the back pointer: verb, noun. The cost grows with T times K squared, not K to the T.
Replace max with sum and you get the forward algorithm, which adds up to zero point two four four eight.
With tagged data, an HMM learns by counting. Noun to noun three times, noun to verb seven times: zero point three and zero point seven.
A zero count would zero a whole path, so we smooth.
Its real weakness: an emission sees one word given one tag. Capital letters, suffixes and neighbouring words are hard to add.
A conditional random field scores whole label sequences given the input, so its features may overlap freely.
Unary scores: can prefers noun, fish prefers verb. Alone, they pick noun verb.
Add one transition score: verb followed by noun gets log eight. Now the path weights are two, four, eight and two.
Z adds up all paths: sixteen. Verb noun gets eight sixteenths, one half. Label compatibility changed the decision.
If verb noun is gold, the loss is log Z minus the gold score: log two. To decode you take the max. Z needs the sum.
For entities, some transitions are illegal: outside to I person, or a sentence starting with I person.
A learned score only discourages them. A hard constraint sets them to minus infinity, so their probability is exactly zero.
A neural tagger reads the whole sentence and gives each token scores. A softmax head decides each token alone. A CRF on top decodes them together.
So: an HMM models words and tags jointly. A softmax head labels each token from context. A CRF scores the whole sequence. Pick by assumptions, and evaluate spans.
